title: Public libraries retain broad legitimacy by functioning as information, technology, learning, and community infrastructure
source_unit: Knight Foundation and NORC at the University of Chicago survey of U.S. adults, May 14-18, 2026
geography: United States; adults ages 18 and older and perceptions of local public libraries

observations.period: May 14-18, 2026; public-library value and essential-service status

denominator.unit: U.S. adults ages 18 and older in the NORC AmeriSpeak Omnibus survey

essential_or_valuable.unit: percent viewing their local public library as an essential or valuable public service

essential.unit: percent viewing their local public library as an essential public service

valuable_not_essential.unit: percent viewing their local public library as valuable but not essential

neither.unit: percent saying their local public library is neither valuable nor essential

cross_group_breadth.value: a majority in every measured age, race, party, and income group viewed local libraries as essential

observations.method: NORC AmeriSpeak Omnibus web and telephone interviews conducted in English and Spanish; overall margin of sampling error plus or minus 3.9 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.
observations.uncertainty: This is a cross-sectional perception survey funded by Knight Foundation; perceived value is not observed usage, service quality, fiscal return, or proof that every library performs equally.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults ages 18 and older across measured demographic, partisan, and income groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Broad legitimacy may reflect symbolic attachment, expected availability, or general support for public goods; it does not establish that people use their local branch or support every program and funding level.

observations.period: May 14-18, 2026; services and community functions valued

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Knight-NORC survey

books_media_information.unit: percent rating access to books, media, and information as extremely or very valuable to the community

neighborhood_place.unit: percent rating a neighborhood place to spend time outside home or work as extremely or very valuable

classes_events.unit: percent rating free classes, activities, and events as extremely or very valuable

computers_internet.unit: percent rating computers, internet access, and technology help as extremely or very valuable

job_and_public_service_help.unit: percent rating help with job searches and navigating public services as extremely or very valuable

multi_function_institution.value: libraries are valued simultaneously as information, technology, learning, work-navigation, and third-place infrastructure

observations.method: Descriptive survey ratings of local library services and community functions.
observations.uncertainty: The measures capture perceived community value and do not establish service availability, reach, quality, frequency, or effects on employment, digital access, learning, or social connection.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults evaluating multiple local-library functions.
observations.counterinterpretation: High perceived value for a service does not mean the library is the preferred or sufficient provider; households may use schools, nonprofits, commercial internet, employers, or government agencies instead.

observations.period: May 14-18, 2026; perceived community value and funding-cut impact

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Knight-NORC survey

community_value_high.unit: percent saying their local public library is extremely or very valuable to their community

community_value_somewhat.unit: percent saying their local public library is somewhat valuable to their community

community_value_not.unit: percent saying their local public library is not valuable to their community

cuts_any_impact.unit: percent saying budget cuts forcing reduced library hours, programs, or services would affect their community

cuts_major.unit: percent expecting a major community impact from library-service cuts

cuts_minor.unit: percent expecting a minor community impact from library-service cuts

observations.method: Cross-sectional NORC survey asking adults to assess community value and a hypothetical local-library budget-cut scenario.
observations.uncertainty: The budget-cut item is a perceived hypothetical impact, not an observed funding change, service reduction, usage loss, or economic evaluation.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults and their perceptions of local community infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: People can value libraries and still accept cuts under fiscal pressure; reported impact does not specify which services, populations, or places would be most affected.

observations.period: May 14-18, 2026; subgroup differences in library valuation

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Knight-NORC survey; subgroup comparisons reported by the source

education_age_pattern.value: college graduates and adults age 30 and older were more likely than adults without a degree and younger adults to recognize personal/community value and anticipate an impact from funding cuts

gender_pattern.value: women were consistently more positive toward libraries, their services, and their potential community impact than men

partisan_pattern.value: Democrats were more likely than Republicans to recognize personal and community value, strongly support services, and see major impact from cuts

legitimacy_distribution.value: broad institutional legitimacy coexists with uneven intensity of valuation across education, age, gender, and party groups

observations.method: Published subgroup comparisons from the Knight-NORC survey; no causal or experimental assignment.
observations.uncertainty: The public fact sheet does not provide all subgroup sample sizes, estimates, or multivariable controls; differences should not be interpreted as effects of education, age, gender, or party identity.
observations.subgroup: Adults grouped by education, age, gender, and self-identified party affiliation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Subgroup differences may reflect local library availability, community context, household needs, political identity, or survey response patterns rather than different underlying library service value.

related_sources.claim: IMLS Public Libraries Survey provides national descriptive administrative data on library systems, facilities, staffing, finance, and usage.
Knight-NORC fact sheet provides survey methodology, 1,047-adult sample, field dates, margin of error, service-value ratings, and subgroup comparisons.

boundary: This record adds a shared-institution mechanism: public libraries retain broad legitimacy because people value them as information, technology, learning, work-navigation, and community-space infrastructure, while intensity of valuation varies across groups. It does not establish usage, service quality, fiscal return, causal trust, or the realized effects of funding cuts.
